package_info.package_name: AgentTesla Christmas Campaign / Die Hard-themed Batch+PowerShell Dropper
package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via phishing email attachments, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (malicious executables and scripts, not versioned packages)
package_info.why_malicious: This campaign leverages phishing emails with holiday themes to deliver malware, including AgentTesla infostealer and a Die Hard-themed dropper. The attack uses malicious executables and scripts to open backdoors, exfiltrate credentials, perform keylogging, and enable remote control of infected systems. The payloads include a multi-stage loader using obfuscated AutoIt scripts, in-memory shellcode execution, process injection, and a batch file that downloads and executes a PowerShell-based reverse shell.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Upon execution, drops fkkvzetzm.exe, jfwxswcu.au3, igqyivch.prc, and kywyozha.x into %usertemp%, then launches fkkvzetzm.exe (AutoIt3) with jfwxswcu.au3 as argument.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Windows executable (drops AutoIt script and binaries)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At user-execution, the executable drops multiple files with randomized names into the user's temp directory, launches an obfuscated AutoIt script via a dropped executable, and initiates a multi-stage malware loader, resulting in further payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and executing multiple files with random names, especially obfuscated scripts, is a common malware staging and evasion technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate executables from trusted sources do not drop and execute obfuscated scripts or unknown binaries in temp directories without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software installers may unpack files, but do not drop obfuscated scripts or random binaries to temp for covert execution.
key_indicators: Obfuscated AutoIt script dropped and executed
Multiple files with random names dropped to temp directory
Execution chain designed to evade detection and facilitate multi-stage loading

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Obfuscated AutoIt script reads and deobfuscates igqyivch.prc (shellcode), allocates memory via VirtualAlloc, loads shellcode, which then loads kywyozha.x into memory.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the AutoIt script deobfuscates and loads shellcode from a dropped file into memory using VirtualAlloc, then executes the shellcode, which in turn loads an additional executable payload into memory, enabling in-memory execution and evasion of disk-based detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: In-memory loading of shellcode and executables is a hallmark of advanced malware seeking to evade disk-based detection and forensic analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate AutoIt scripts do not load and execute shellcode or additional binaries from obfuscated sources, nor do they allocate memory for direct code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing frameworks and red team tools may use similar in-memory execution techniques for authorized testing.
key_indicators: Obfuscated script deobfuscating and executing shellcode
Use of VirtualAlloc for memory allocation and code execution
No user-facing functionality or legitimate application logic

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Shellcode loads kywyozha.x into memory, launches a copy of the running process, checks for 64bit process, copies ntdll.dll into memory, checks for API hooks, and injects kywyozha.x into the new process.
malicious_snippets.code_language: Shellcode (x86/x64 assembly, executed via AutoIt loader)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the shellcode loads an additional payload into memory, spawns a new process, performs anti-analysis checks such as verifying process architecture and scanning for API hooks, copies ntdll.dll into memory, and injects the main payload into the new process, enabling stealthy execution and evasion of security tools.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Process injection, anti-analysis checks, and in-memory DLL loading are advanced evasion and persistence techniques used by sophisticated malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not inject code into other processes, perform anti-forensics checks, or copy system DLLs into memory for stealth.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some security tools or debuggers may use process injection for analysis or monitoring, but not for covert payload delivery.
key_indicators: Process injection into newly spawned process
In-memory copy of ntdll.dll and API hook detection
Anti-forensics and anti-EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) behavior

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: AgentTesla infostealer variant: downloads/deletes files, steals credentials from browsers, FTP, email apps, performs keylogging, communicates with C2 via Telegram API (hxxps://api.telegram[.]org/bot5018340186:AAFKw8ktzY7O_6e1fhgEWq27H2aE-rsBGjA/).
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the injected payload exfiltrates credentials from browsers, FTP, and email clients, performs keylogging, enables remote file operations, and communicates with a Telegram-based command and control server to transmit stolen data and receive attacker instructions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Credential theft, keylogging, and C2 communication via Telegram API are core infostealer behaviors and indicate active data exfiltration and remote control.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not exfiltrate credentials, perform keylogging, or communicate with Telegram C2 servers without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools may have similar capabilities, but only with user knowledge and consent, and not via covert channels.
key_indicators: Credential exfiltration from browsers, FTP, and email clients
Telegram API C2 communication for data exfiltration and remote commands

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Batch file displays image7.jpg.jpg and loads/executes PowerShell code from hxxps://pastebin[.]com/raw/PeJLUFC4.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At user-execution, the batch file masquerades as an image, displays a decoy image to the user, and downloads and executes a remote PowerShell script from pastebin, initiating the next stage of the attack.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Batch files disguised as images that download and execute remote scripts are a classic malware delivery method designed to trick users and evade basic file extension checks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Image files should not contain executable code or download and execute scripts; batch files should not masquerade as images.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT automation may use batch files to run scripts, but not disguised as images or for covert remote code execution.
key_indicators: Remote PowerShell script execution from pastebin
Decoy image display to mislead the user

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: PowerShell script creates a reverse shell backdoor, allowing execution of arbitrary PowerShell commands from the attacker's system.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell script establishes a reverse shell connection to the attacker's system, enabling the attacker to execute arbitrary PowerShell commands on the victim's machine and maintain persistent remote access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reverse shells are a primary method for attackers to gain unauthorized remote control over victim systems, often used for post-exploitation and lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: PowerShell scripts should not create unauthorized remote access channels or allow arbitrary command execution from external sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red teamers and system administrators may use reverse shells for authorized testing or remote support, but not via disguised image files or without user awareness.
key_indicators: Reverse shell creation enabling remote access
PowerShell code hosted on pastebin for dynamic retrieval

attack_chain.action: User receives phishing email with malicious attachment (holiday-themed).
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens attachment, triggering malware execution.

attack_chain.action: User executes malicious file (either .exe or disguised batch file).
Malware loader drops and executes obfuscated scripts and shellcode (AgentTesla chain) or downloads and runs PowerShell (Die Hard chain).
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload is loaded into memory or reverse shell is established.

attack_chain.action: Payload executes: AgentTesla infostealer exfiltrates data and communicates with C2, or PowerShell reverse shell gives attacker remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data exfiltration, remote control, and further exploitation.

behavioral_signatures: Executable or script drops multiple files with random names to temp directories
Obfuscated AutoIt scripts that deobfuscate and execute shellcode in memory
In-memory loading of executables and system DLLs (e.g., ntdll.dll)
Process injection and anti-analysis checks (API hook detection, in-memory DLL copy)
Credential theft from browsers, FTP, and email clients
Keylogging and unauthorized access to keyboard input
Batch files disguised as images (e.g., .jpg.bat) that download and execute PowerShell scripts
PowerShell scripts establishing reverse shells and enabling arbitrary command execution
file_indicators: Files with random names in %usertemp% (e.g., fkkvzetzm.exe, jfwxswcu.au3, igqyivch.prc, kywyozha.x)
Archives containing executables or disguised batch files (e.g., good_time.zip, new designs.gz)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of files with suspicious or double extensions (e.g., .jpg.bat), especially when originating from email attachments. Detect batch files or scripts that download and execute remote PowerShell code, particularly from pastebin or similar services. Flag in-memory execution of shellcode, process injection, and use of obfuscated AutoIt scripts. Watch for outbound connections to known C2 infrastructure, such as Telegram API endpoints and pastebin links. Alert on credential access, keylogging activity, and attempts to exfiltrate data via unusual network channels. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify multi-stage loader activity and infostealer deployment.
